items.stem: Define the term "competitive market".
items.answer: A market with many buyers and sellers, none of whom can influence the price
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a market with many buyers and sellers, none of whom can influence the price. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why queues and empty shelves suggest that a price is below equilibrium.
items.answer: Queues show that quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the current price (excess demand); in a free market price would rise to ration the good.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Queues show that quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the current price (excess demand); in a free market price would rise to ration the good. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between excess supply and excess demand.
items.answer: Excess demand occurs below equilibrium, where Qd > Qs, and pushes price up; excess supply occurs above equilibrium, where Qs > Qd, and pushes price down.
items.markingKey: Excess demand occurs below equilibrium, where Qd > Qs, and pushes price up; excess supply occurs above equilibrium, where Qs > Qd, and pushes price down. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

Hypothetical market data for mangoes in Accra (per week): at GH₵10 per kg, Qd = 900 kg and Qs = 300 kg; at GH₵15, Qd = 700 kg and Qs = 500 kg; at GH₵20, Qd = 600 kg and Qs = 600 kg; at GH₵25, Qd = 500 kg and Qs = 700 kg.
— Hypothetical data

Using the data, identify the equilibrium price and quantity and describe the market situation at GH₵10.
items.answer: Equilibrium: GH₵20 and 600 kg (Qd = Qs). At GH₵10 there is excess demand of 600 kg (900 − 300), so price will rise.
items.markingKey: Equilibrium: GH₵20 and 600 kg (Qd = Qs). At GH₵10 there is excess demand of 600 kg (900 − 300), so price will rise. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how excess demand and excess supply are eliminated in a competitive market.
items.answer: Diagram: downward-sloping D and upward-sloping S intersecting at Pe, Qe. At P1 above Pe, Qs > Qd: excess supply; sellers cut prices, moving along both curves to Pe. At P2 below Pe, Qd > Qs: excess demand; buyers bid up price to Pe. At Pe, Qd = Qs and the market clears.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: downward-sloping D and upward-sloping S intersecting at Pe, Qe. At P1 above Pe, Qs > Qd: excess supply; sellers cut prices, moving along both curves to Pe. At P2 below Pe, Qd > Qs: excess demand; buyers bid up price to Pe. At Pe, Qd = Qs and the market clears. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the shortage of PlayStation 5 consoles in 2020-2021 shows excess demand.
items.answer: Sony's launch price was fixed while supply was limited by chip shortages; consoles sold out instantly and resold online at far higher prices. At the fixed launch price Qd far exceeded Qs, so resale prices rose towards the market-clearing level.
items.markingKey: Context (Sony's launch price was fixed while supply was limited by chip shortages; consoles sold out instantly and resold online at far higher prices.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: At the fixed launch price Qd far exceeded Qs, so resale prices rose towards the market-clearing level. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to excess demand.

items.stem: Using a diagram, explain how the price mechanism eliminates a surplus in the market for apples after an unusually large harvest.
items.answer: The large harvest shifts supply right; at the original price Qs > Qd; sellers cut prices to clear stock; as price falls, quantity demanded rises and quantity supplied falls along S2 until a new, lower equilibrium price is reached with higher quantity.
items.markingKey: The large harvest shifts supply right; at the original price Qs > Qd; sellers cut prices to clear stock; as price falls, quantity demanded rises and quantity supplied falls along S2 until a new, lower equilibrium price is reached with higher quantity.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that Shortages are always a sign that a market is failing?
items.answer: Persistent shortages suggest market or government failure, but temporary shortages are part of normal market adjustment.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: persistent shortages show the price mechanism is not working; may be caused by price controls. Arguments against: temporary shortages occur as markets adjust to new equilibria; firms may deliberately price below equilibrium (concerts) for reputation; supply shocks take time to resolve. Supported judgement: Persistent shortages suggest market or government failure, but temporary shortages are part of normal market adjustment. Level 1 (1-3) little understanding.

items.stem: Explain how a market with excess supply moves to equilibrium.
items.answer: Firms cannot sell all their output at the current price, so they cut prices; as price falls, quantity demanded rises and quantity supplied falls (movements along the curves) until Qd = Qs at the equilibrium price.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Firms cannot sell all their output at the current price, so they cut prices; as price falls, quantity demanded rises and quantity supplied falls (movements along the curves) until Qd = Qs at the equilibrium price. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "At equilibrium every consumer who wants the good gets it." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: At equilibrium every consumer willing and able to pay the equilibrium price can buy; those unwilling or unable to pay do not.
items.markingKey: At equilibrium every consumer willing and able to pay the equilibrium price can buy; those unwilling or unable to pay do not. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Markets always move quickly to equilibrium." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Many markets adjust quickly, but stickiness, regulation and imperfect information mean disequilibrium can persist.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: excess demand and supply create strong price pressures; online markets adjust prices instantly (dynamic pricing). Arguments against: prices can be sticky (menus, contracts, social norms – concert tickets); government price controls prevent adjustment; information is imperfect and expectations may destabilise prices (housing). Supported judgement: Many markets adjust quickly, but stickiness, regulation and imperfect information mean disequilibrium can persist. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Comparing the original and the new equilibrium after a change, without analysing the path between them"?
items.answer: comparative statics
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of comparative statics.

items.stem: "When demand rises, supply rises too because firms see more customers." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Firms respond to the higher price by increasing quantity supplied – a movement along the supply curve; supply itself does not shift.
items.markingKey: Firms respond to the higher price by increasing quantity supplied – a movement along the supply curve; supply itself does not shift. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why an increase in both demand and supply has an uncertain effect on price.
items.answer: The demand increase pushes price up while the supply increase pushes it down; the net effect depends on which shift is larger.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The demand increase pushes price up while the supply increase pushes it down; the net effect depends on which shift is larger. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Tomás writes: "When demand rises, supply rises too because firms see more customers." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Firms respond to the higher price by increasing quantity supplied – a movement along the supply curve; supply itself does not shift.
items.markingKey: Firms respond to the higher price by increasing quantity supplied – a movement along the supply curve; supply itself does not shift. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

In 2023 the world price of olive oil reached a record high of over €8,000 per tonne after two years of drought in Spain, which produces around 40% of the world's olive oil. Meanwhile, rising interest in the Mediterranean diet continued to increase demand in Asia and North America.
— Extract based on reporting of the olive oil market

Using a diagram, explain the changes in the olive oil market described in the extract.
items.answer: Drought shifted supply left and rising health-driven demand shifted demand right; both raise price, so the equilibrium price rose sharply; the effect on quantity is uncertain (likely fell given the large supply shock).
items.markingKey: Drought shifted supply left and rising health-driven demand shifted demand right; both raise price, so the equilibrium price rose sharply; the effect on quantity is uncertain (likely fell given the large supply shock). Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Explain, with the help of a fully labelled diagram, the effect of a fall in the price of a complement on the equilibrium of a market such as gaming headsets.
items.answer: Diagram: a fall in the price of consoles increases their quantity demanded, so demand for headsets shifts right from D1 to D2; excess demand at P1 pushes price up to P2 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q2 along S.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: a fall in the price of consoles increases their quantity demanded, so demand for headsets shifts right from D1 to D2; excess demand at P1 pushes price up to P2 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q2 along S. items.stem: Using diagrams, explain the likely effects on the market for beef of (i) a rise in the price of cattle feed and (ii) growing popularity of plant-based burgers, occurring at the same time.
items.answer: (i) supply shifts left; (ii) demand shifts left. Quantity falls for certain; price change depends on relative shifts. Draw D1/D2 and S1/S2 with new equilibrium.
items.markingKey: (i) supply shifts left; (ii) demand shifts left. Quantity falls for certain; price change depends on relative shifts. Draw D1/D2 and S1/S2 with new equilibrium.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that Supply and demand analysis can accurately predict changes in the prices of primary commodities.
items.answer: The model predicts the direction of changes well but rarely the size, because many simultaneous influences act on commodity markets.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shows the direction of price changes after shocks; explains volatility when demand and supply are inelastic. Arguments against: many shifts happen at once and are hard to measure; speculation and expectations move prices; government stockpiles and export bans interfere. Supported judgement: The model predicts the direction of changes well but rarely the size, because many simultaneous influences act on commodity markets. items.stem: Explain why a fall in the price of a substitute reduces both the equilibrium price and quantity of a good.
items.answer: Consumers switch to the cheaper substitute, so demand for the good shifts left; at the original price there is excess supply, and price and quantity fall to a new equilibrium.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Consumers switch to the cheaper substitute, so demand for the good shifts left; at the original price there is excess supply, and price and quantity fall to a new equilibrium. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that if supply falls, price rises, which then reduces demand, so the demand curve shifts left. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A higher price reduces quantity demanded – a movement along the demand curve; demand (the curve) does not shift because of a change in the good's own price.
items.markingKey: A higher price reduces quantity demanded – a movement along the demand curve; demand (the curve) does not shift because of a change in the good's own price. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The role of price changes in conveying information to buyers and sellers about where resources are wanted"?
items.answer: signalling function of price
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of signalling function of price.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the price mechanism might be considered an 'invisible hand'.
items.answer: Without central direction, self-interested buyers and sellers respond to prices; this coordinates millions of decisions and allocates resources to their most valued uses, as Adam Smith described.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Without central direction, self-interested buyers and sellers respond to prices; this coordinates millions of decisions and allocates resources to their most valued uses, as Adam Smith described. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that Allocative efficiency means consumers pay the lowest possible price. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Allocative efficiency means resources produce what society values most, where MB = MC; the price is the market price at that point, not the lowest possible price.
items.markingKey: Allocative efficiency means resources produce what society values most, where MB = MC; the price is the market price at that point, not the lowest possible price. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how rising lithium prices between 2020 and 2022 illustrate the signalling and incentive functions of price.
items.answer: The price rise signalled that lithium was increasingly scarce relative to demand from battery makers; higher profits gave mining firms the incentive to open new mines in Australia, Chile and Argentina, increasing quantity supplied.
items.markingKey: The price rise signalled that lithium was increasingly scarce relative to demand from battery makers; higher profits gave mining firms the incentive to open new mines in Australia, Chile and Argentina, increasing quantity supplied.

items.stem: "The price mechanism ensures goods go to those who need them most." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Price allocates goods to those most willing and able to pay, which depends on income; those in greatest need may be unable to pay, which is why governments intervene for equity.
items.markingKey: Price allocates goods to those most willing and able to pay, which depends on income; those in greatest need may be unable to pay, which is why governments intervene for equity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that the price mechanism allocates resources fairly.
items.answer: The price mechanism is efficient in many markets but not necessarily fair; equity requires additional policies.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: prices reflect what people are willing to pay; voluntary exchange benefits both sides. Arguments against: willingness to pay depends on income, which is unequal; necessities may be unaffordable for the poor; market power and externalities distort prices. Supported judgement: The price mechanism is efficient in many markets but not necessarily fair; equity requires additional policies.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The allocation of resources that maximises social surplus, achieved when the price consumers pay equals the marginal cost of production (MB = MC)"?
items.answer: allocative efficiency
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of allocative efficiency.

items.answer: Price allocates goods to those most willing and able to pay, which depends on income; those in greatest need may be unable to pay, which is why governments intervene for equity.
items.markingKey: Price allocates goods to those most willing and able to pay, which depends on income; those in greatest need may be unable to pay, which is why governments intervene for equity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "consumer surplus".
items.answer: The difference between the highest price consumers are willing to pay and the price they actually pay, shown by the area below the demand curve and above the price
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the difference between the highest price consumers are willing to pay and the price they actually pay, shown by the area below the demand curve and above the price. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between welfare loss and social surplus.
items.answer: Social surplus is the total benefit to society from producing and consuming a good (CS + PS); welfare loss is the part of potential social surplus lost when output is not at the efficient level.
items.markingKey: Social surplus is the total benefit to society from producing and consuming a good (CS + PS); welfare loss is the part of potential social surplus lost when output is not at the efficient level. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that social surplus is maximised when consumer surplus is maximised. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Social surplus is the sum of consumer and producer surplus, maximised at the competitive equilibrium; maximising consumer surplus alone (e.g. a very low price) would reduce output and producer surplus.
items.markingKey: Social surplus is the sum of consumer and producer surplus, maximised at the competitive equilibrium; maximising consumer surplus alone (e.g. a very low price) would reduce output and producer surplus. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using a diagram, explain the effect on consumer surplus, producer surplus and social surplus of an increase in supply resulting from new technology.
items.answer: Supply shifts right; price falls, quantity rises; consumer surplus increases (larger triangle below D above the lower price); producer surplus changes (may rise as quantity rises); social surplus rises because the efficient output is larger.
items.markingKey: Supply shifts right; price falls, quantity rises; consumer surplus increases (larger triangle below D above the lower price); producer surplus changes (may rise as quantity rises); social surplus rises because the efficient output is larger.

items.stem: On a demand and supply diagram, where is consumer surplus shown?
options: The area between the two curves to the right of equilibrium
The area below the demand curve and above the market price
The area above the supply curve and below the market price
The area under the supply curve
items.answer: The area below the demand curve and above the market price
items.markingKey: B. Consumers value those units more than they pay.

items.stem: Data from a consumer survey and from producers in Lisbon give the demand function Qd = 58 − 2P and the supply function Qs = −5 + P for coffee (P in $; Q in thousands per month). The equilibrium price is $21 and quantity 16. Calculate producer surplus.
items.markingKey: Supply meets the price axis at 5; PS = ½ × (21 − 5) × 16 = 128. [1] intercept [1] area

items.stem: Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = −20 + 4P. What is the equilibrium price?
Rafael writes: "To find equilibrium quantity, substitute the equilibrium price into the demand function only, because supply does not matter." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Either function gives the same quantity at equilibrium; substituting into both is a useful check, and supply matters as much as demand in finding the price.
items.markingKey: Either function gives the same quantity at equilibrium; substituting into both is a useful check, and supply matters as much as demand in finding the price. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why it is good practice to check an equilibrium calculation by substituting the price into both functions.
items.answer: Both functions must give the same quantity at the equilibrium price; if they do not, an arithmetic error has been made. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.stem: Demand is Qd = 400 − 10P and supply is Qs = 100 + 5P. Calculate equilibrium price and quantity.
With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how to plot the linear functions Qd = 120 − 4P and Qs = −30 + 6P and identify the equilibrium.
items.answer: Diagram: P on the vertical axis; demand meets Q axis at 120 and P axis at 30; supply meets P axis at 5 and passes through (Q = 30, P = 10). They intersect where 120 − 4P = −30 + 6P: P = 15, Q = 60. Label Pe = 15, Qe = 60.

items.stem: Given Qd = 240 − 6P and Qs = −60 + 4P, calculate the equilibrium, then calculate the new equilibrium if a subsidy shifts supply to Qs = −20 + 4P, and explain the change.
items.answer: Original: 300 = 10P ⇒ P = 30, Q = 60. New: 260 = 10P ⇒ P = 26, Q = 84. Supply increase lowers price by $4 and raises quantity by 24.
items.markingKey: Original: 300 = 10P ⇒ P = 30, Q = 60. New: 260 = 10P ⇒ P = 26, Q = 84. Supply increase lowers price by $4 and raises quantity by 24.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that algebraic calculation of equilibrium is more useful than diagrams in economic analysis.
items.answer: Algebra and diagrams complement each other: algebra quantifies effects, diagrams explain them.

items.stem: Which of the following brings a market back to equilibrium when there is excess demand?
options: A shift of the supply curve to the left
A rise in price that reduces quantity demanded and increases quantity supplied
A shift of the demand curve to the right
items.answer: A rise in price that reduces quantity demanded and increases quantity supplied
items.markingKey: B. Price rises, moving along both curves until Qd = Qs.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "simultaneous shifts"?
options: A movement to a new equilibrium price and quantity caused by a shift in demand, supply or both
The equilibrium price at which all the units that producers want to sell are bought
A situation where demand and supply both shift, so the effect on either price or quantity is indeterminate unless the sizes of the shifts are known
The role of price changes in conveying information to buyers and sellers about where resources are wanted
items.answer: A situation where demand and supply both shift, so the effect on either price or quantity is indeterminate unless the sizes of the shifts are known
items.markingKey: C. "simultaneous shifts" is a situation where demand and supply both shift, so the effect on either price or quantity is indeterminate unless the sizes of the shifts are known.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "rationing function of price"?
options: A movement to a new equilibrium price and quantity caused by a shift in demand, supply or both
The loss of social surplus that results when output is not at the allocatively efficient level
The role of price in allocating scarce goods to those willing and able to pay
The difference between the price producers receive and the lowest price they would accept, shown by the area above the supply curve and below the price
items.answer: The role of price in allocating scarce goods to those willing and able to pay
items.markingKey: C. "rationing function of price" is the role of price in allocating scarce goods to those willing and able to pay.

items.stem: Distinguish between consumer surplus and producer surplus.
items.answer: Consumer surplus is the benefit to buyers above what they pay (below demand, above price); producer surplus is the benefit to sellers above their minimum acceptable price (above supply, below price).

items.answer: The signalling function is the information prices convey about scarcity and demand; the incentive function is the motivation prices give producers and consumers to change behaviour.

items.stem: Using the 2022 surge in natural gas prices in Europe as an example, explain the effect of a fall in supply on equilibrium.
items.answer: Russia cut pipeline gas deliveries to Europe and European gas prices rose to many times their previous level. Supply shifted left while demand was inelastic, so the equilibrium price rose sharply and quantity fell modestly.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how the price mechanism reallocates resources in response to an increase in demand, using the signalling and incentive functions of price.
items.answer: Diagram: D1 shifts right to D2; excess demand at P1; price rises to P2 (signal of scarcity); higher price makes production more profitable, so firms increase quantity supplied along S from Q1 to Q2 (incentive); the higher price also rations the good to those willing and able to pay.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: D1 shifts right to D2; excess demand at P1; price rises to P2 (signal of scarcity); higher price makes production more profitable, so firms increase quantity supplied along S from Q1 to Q2 (incentive); the higher price also rations the good to those willing and able to pay. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Five consumers are willing to pay $12, $10, $8, $6 and $4 for one unit each of a good selling at $7. Calculate total consumer surplus.

Data from a consumer survey and from producers in Kuala Lumpur give the demand function Qd = 50 − 5P and the supply function Qs = −10 + 5P for avocados (P in $; Q in thousands per month). Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity.

Data from a consumer survey and from producers in Kuala Lumpur give the demand function Qd = 25 − P and the supply function Qs = −5 + 5P for smartphones (P in $; Q in thousands per month). The price is currently $6. Calculate the size of the surplus and explain how the market will adjust to equilibrium, stating the equilibrium price and quantity.
items.answer: excess supply (surplus) of 6; equilibrium P = $5, Q = 20
items.markingKey: Qd = 19, Qs = 25, difference 6 [1]; price falls, causing movements along both curves [1]; 25 − 1P = -5 + 5P ⇒ P = 5 [1], Q = 20 [1].

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that governments should intervene whenever a supply shock causes a large rise in the price of a necessity.
items.answer: Intervention can be justified for necessities, but targeted support is generally better than measures that blunt the price signal.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: protects low-income households; prevents hardship and social unrest. Arguments against: price signals encourage more supply and less waste; intervention (price ceilings) may cause shortages; targeted transfers may be better than general controls. Supported judgement: Intervention can be justified for necessities, but targeted support is generally better than measures that blunt the price signal.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, discuss the claim that the price mechanism is the most efficient way to allocate scarce resources.
items.answer: The price mechanism is efficient in competitive markets without market failure, but in many important markets intervention is needed for efficiency and equity.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: prices coordinate decentralised information (Hayek); incentives encourage efficiency and innovation; maximises social surplus in competitive markets without externalities. Arguments against: market failure: externalities, public goods, information problems; inequitable outcomes – rationing by ability to pay; market power distorts prices. Judgement: The price mechanism is efficient in competitive markets without market failure, but in many important markets intervention is needed for efficiency and equity. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. items.stem: To what extent is it true that Consumer surplus is a useful measure of the benefit consumers gain from a market?
items.answer: Consumer surplus is a valuable conceptual measure for policy evaluation, but it must be used with caution because it depends on ability to pay and estimates of demand.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: measures willingness to pay above price; helps evaluate policies such as taxes and price controls. Arguments against: willingness to pay depends on income; hard to measure demand curves accurately; ignores external benefits and behavioural biases. Supported judgement: Consumer surplus is a valuable conceptual measure for policy evaluation, but it must be used with caution because it depends on ability to pay and estimates of demand. items.stem: "Algebraic calculation of equilibrium is more useful than diagrams in economic analysis." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Algebra and diagrams complement each other: algebra quantifies effects, diagrams explain them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: precise numerical answers; allows calculation of revenue, surplus and tax effects. Arguments against: diagrams show relationships and direction of change clearly; algebra depends on knowing the functions, which are estimates; both are needed to communicate analysis. Supported judgement: Algebra and diagrams complement each other: algebra quantifies effects, diagrams explain them. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The equilibrium price at which all the units that producers want to sell are bought"?
items.answer: market-clearing price
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of market-clearing price.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "simultaneous shifts".
items.answer: A situation where demand and supply both shift, so the effect on either price or quantity is indeterminate unless the sizes of the shifts are known
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a situation where demand and supply both shift, so the effect on either price or quantity is indeterminate unless the sizes of the shifts are known. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "rationing function of price".
items.answer: The role of price in allocating scarce goods to those willing and able to pay
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the role of price in allocating scarce goods to those willing and able to pay. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why producing more than the equilibrium quantity reduces social surplus.
items.answer: Beyond equilibrium, the cost of each extra unit (supply curve) exceeds the benefit consumers gain from it (demand curve); producing these units subtracts from social surplus, creating a welfare loss.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Beyond equilibrium, the cost of each extra unit (supply curve) exceeds the benefit consumers gain from it (demand curve); producing these units subtracts from social surplus, creating a welfare loss. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why the equilibrium price is found by setting Qd equal to Qs.
items.answer: Equilibrium is where the quantity consumers want to buy equals the quantity firms want to sell; only at that price is there no excess demand or supply.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Equilibrium is where the quantity consumers want to buy equals the quantity firms want to sell; only at that price is there no excess demand or supply. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between scarcity and a shortage.
items.answer: A shortage is a temporary market condition where Qd > Qs at a given price; scarcity is the permanent condition that resources are limited relative to wants.
items.markingKey: A shortage is a temporary market condition where Qd > Qs at a given price; scarcity is the permanent condition that resources are limited relative to wants. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a fall in supply and a rise in demand.
items.answer: Both raise the equilibrium price, but a rise in demand increases equilibrium quantity while a fall in supply reduces it.
items.markingKey: Both raise the equilibrium price, but a rise in demand increases equilibrium quantity while a fall in supply reduces it. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why allocative efficiency occurs at the competitive market equilibrium.
items.answer: At equilibrium the demand curve (marginal benefit) meets the supply curve (marginal cost), so the last unit produced is valued exactly at its cost; producing less or more would reduce social surplus.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: At equilibrium the demand curve (marginal benefit) meets the supply curve (marginal cost), so the last unit produced is valued exactly at its cost; producing less or more would reduce social surplus. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Social surplus is maximised when consumer surplus is maximised." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Social surplus is the sum of consumer and producer surplus, maximised at the competitive equilibrium; maximising consumer surplus alone (e.g. a very low price) would reduce output and producer surplus.
items.markingKey: Social surplus is the sum of consumer and producer surplus, maximised at the competitive equilibrium; maximising consumer surplus alone (e.g. a very low price) would reduce output and producer surplus. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to estimating the effect of a new low-cost airline route, explain how it illustrates calculating equilibrium from linear functions.
items.answer: An airport authority estimates linear demand and supply for seats on a route to forecast price and passenger numbers when a new airline enters. Entry adds to supply (raising c), so solving the new equations predicts a lower fare and more passengers.
items.markingKey: Context (An airport authority estimates linear demand and supply for seats on a route to forecast price and passenger numbers when a new airline enters.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Entry adds to supply (raising c), so solving the new equations predicts a lower fare and more passengers. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to calculating equilibrium from linear functions.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate how excess demand and excess supply are eliminated in a competitive market, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Diagram: downward-sloping D and upward-sloping S intersecting at Pe, Qe. At P1 above Pe, Qs > Qd: excess supply; sellers cut prices, moving along both curves to Pe. At P2 below Pe, Qd > Qs: excess demand; buyers bid up price to Pe. At Pe, Qd = Qs and the market clears.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: downward-sloping D and upward-sloping S intersecting at Pe, Qe. At P1 above Pe, Qs > Qd: excess supply; sellers cut prices, moving along both curves to Pe. At P2 below Pe, Qd > Qs: excess demand; buyers bid up price to Pe. At Pe, Qd = Qs and the market clears. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Data from a consumer survey and from producers in Hanoi give the demand function Qd = 114 − 2P and the supply function Qs = −30 + 6P for smartphones (P in $; Q in thousands per month). Following a health scare, the demand function becomes Qd = 106 − 2P. Calculate the original and new equilibrium price and quantity, and comment on the direction of change.
items.answer: Original P = $18, Q = 78; new P = $17, Q = 72
items.markingKey: Original: 114 − 2P = −30 + 6P ⇒ P = 18, Q = 78 [1]; new: P = (106 − (-30))/8 = 17, Q = 72 [2]; demand decrease lowers both price and quantity [1].

items.stem: Briefly describe dynamic 'surge pricing' by ride-hailing apps such as Uber and explain what it reveals about the rationing and incentive functions of price.
items.answer: When demand rises at peak times or in bad weather, prices rise automatically; more drivers go online and some passengers wait or travel another way. Higher prices ration rides to those who value them most and give drivers an incentive to supply more rides.
items.markingKey: Context (When demand rises at peak times or in bad weather, prices rise automatically; more drivers go online and some passengers wait or travel another way.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Higher prices ration rides to those who value them most and give drivers an incentive to supply more rides. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the rationing and incentive functions of price.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate consumer surplus, producer surplus and social surplus at the competitive market equilibrium, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Diagram: D and S intersect at Pe, Qe. Consumer surplus: triangle between D and the line Pe, up to Qe. Producer surplus: triangle between Pe and S, up to Qe. Together they form social surplus, which is maximised at Qe where MB (demand) = MC (supply), so the outcome is allocatively efficient.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: D and S intersect at Pe, Qe. Consumer surplus: triangle between D and the line Pe, up to Qe. Producer surplus: triangle between Pe and S, up to Qe. Together they form social surplus, which is maximised at Qe where MB (demand) = MC (supply), so the outcome is allocatively efficient. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate how to plot the linear functions Qd = 120 − 4P and Qs = −30 + 6P and identify the equilibrium, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Diagram: P on the vertical axis; demand meets Q axis at 120 and P axis at 30; supply meets P axis at 5 and passes through (Q = 30, P = 10). They intersect where 120 − 4P = −30 + 6P: P = 15, Q = 60. Label Pe = 15, Qe = 60.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: P on the vertical axis; demand meets Q axis at 120 and P axis at 30; supply meets P axis at 5 and passes through (Q = 30, P = 10). They intersect where 120 − 4P = −30 + 6P: P = 15, Q = 60. Label Pe = 15, Qe = 60. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Tomás writes: "At equilibrium every consumer who wants the good gets it." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: At equilibrium every consumer willing and able to pay the equilibrium price can buy; those unwilling or unable to pay do not.
items.markingKey: At equilibrium every consumer willing and able to pay the equilibrium price can buy; those unwilling or unable to pay do not. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Supply and demand analysis can accurately predict changes in the prices of primary commodities."
items.answer: The model predicts the direction of changes well but rarely the size, because many simultaneous influences act on commodity markets.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shows the direction of price changes after shocks; explains volatility when demand and supply are inelastic. Arguments against: many shifts happen at once and are hard to measure; speculation and expectations move prices; government stockpiles and export bans interfere. Supported judgement: The model predicts the direction of changes well but rarely the size, because many simultaneous influences act on commodity markets.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that calculating equilibrium from linear functions gives policy makers reliable predictions.
items.answer: Linear models are useful for direction and approximate size, but forecasts must be treated as estimates and tested against outcomes.
